changed and that's just not up for
debate. Hey everybody, I'm Dan
McClellan. I'm a scholar of the Bible
and religion and to acknowledge that the
texts of the New Testament have been
changed is not to insist that we haven't
already resolved the overwhelming
majority of those changes because we
have. It's to acknowledge that when we
look at the thousands of different
manuscripts that we have, we can see an
awful lot of differences among them. We
can see that change has been introduced.
The texts have been changed.
But because of all that manuscript
evidence, we can reconstruct
a version of the New Testament that we
can be pretty confident quite closely
matches what came from the pens of the
original authors. And this is why if you
look at a translation of the New
Testament that was published within the
last few decades, they will almost
certainly omit entire verses such as
Matthew 17:21 where it'll just skip over
it in the main body of the text and
you'll have to go to the footnote to
read it and there will usually be a
comment like some ancient authorities
include this, but the earliest
manuscripts don't have it. Something
similar is going on with the story of
the woman and taken in adultery and the
long ending of the Gospel of Mark where
those things are not in the earliest
manuscripts and scholars are pretty
confident that they are secondary
additions. But because of their length
and how embedded in the tradition they
are, they tend to be included in the
main body of the text and the footnote
will point out that these are not in the
earliest manuscripts. So we've been able
to resolve the overwhelming majority of
the changes that we can see being
introduced to the text.
My question is
what changes were introduced that we
have not been able to detect? Because
there's a gap of varying length between
when scholars believe a text of the New
Testament was originally composed and
our earliest manuscript witness to any
given verse from that text. And that gap
is sometimes a matter of just a couple
or a few decades for about 36 or so
words from the Gospel of John to well
over a century for the majority of the
verses of the New Testament. And where
we do have multiple manuscript
witnesses, invariably there are
differences. So I don't think the
assumption is merited that where we lack
any manuscript witnesses, no changes
were introduced. Particularly because in
the earliest years of the circulation of
the manuscript, change is going to be
more difficult to discern and so is
going to be more likely to be
perpetuated. And so while some scholars
assume that we have all the manuscript
evidence that we need to reconstruct the
New Testament exactly as it came from
the pens of the authors, I think it is
far more responsible to assume that
there has been changes introduced to the
texts of the New Testament that we don't
have enough evidence to be able to
detect and we probably never will. And
the fit for this video needs no
